templates.name: Period between independent clauses (second often opens with an introductory phrase)
Conjunctive adverb: semicolon or period on the correct side, comma on the other
Colon after a complete clause before an explanation or specified item
No punctuation with a restrictive clause or restrictive appositive
Dash pair around a supplementary element
Items in a series (commas; semicolons when items contain commas)
Comma or parenthesis pair around a supplementary element
Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
Comma before a trailing nonrestrictive modifier
No punctuation between a verb or preposition and its object
Question versus statement (word order and end mark)

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a with-absolute phrase that could trail the first
items.passage: During the Great Depression, the Austrian town of Wörgl financed public construction projects with its own currency: certificates that lost 1 percent of their value every ______ holders eager to spend them before the next deduction, the certificates circulated rapidly, and local businesses gradually recovered.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “During the Great Depression ... lost 1 percent of their value every month” is a complete sentence. “The certificates circulated rapidly” is the main clause of the next sentence, which opens with the phrase “With holders eager to spend them before the next deduction.” A period after “month” separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: With a comma, the “with” phrase reads as a tail of the first sentence, but “the certificates circulated rapidly” is a second independent clause, so the two clauses are joined by a comma alone.

B.why_wrong: Adding “and” doesn’t fix the problem: “the certificates circulated rapidly” is still a second independent clause joined to the first by a comma alone, so the result is a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the “with” phrase runs into the first clause, and the independent clause “the certificates circulated rapidly” is then joined to it by a comma alone.

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics: Wörgl’s depreciating work certificates, 1932 to 1933). Band 6: a 10-word with-absolute opener that could legally trail clause 1 (“every month, with holders eager ...”), so the splice in A appears only at “the certificates,” 10 words past the blank (1b97cce9, b15724fc shape). No semicolon option (it would be a legal twin) and no “, and with” option (legal). No person named.

fixes: why_wrong A, B and D quoted “the certificates changed hands rapidly”; the passage says “circulated rapidly”; B now leads with the splice

band7.why: Target 6. S1_period on 1b97cce9 and b15724fc: a 10-word with-phrase opener that can trail clause 1, so the splice in A, B and D shows only at “the certificates,” 10 words past the blank; a prepositional opener is the band-6 type. Every wrong option fails on rule (splice or fused).

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a long adjective phrase that could modify the first clause’s last noun
items.passage: In 2007, images from an orbiting ultraviolet telescope revealed that Mira, a red giant star, is trailed by an enormous ______ only at ultraviolet wavelengths and extending approximately 13 light-years, this comet-like tail consists of material that the star has gradually expelled over the past 30,000 years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 2007, images ... revealed that Mira, a red giant star, is trailed by an enormous structure” is a complete sentence. “Visible only at ultraviolet wavelengths and extending approximately 13 light-years” describes “this comet-like tail,” the subject of the next sentence (“this comet-like tail consists of material ...”), so a period is needed after “structure.”

B.why_wrong: The comma lets “visible only at ultraviolet wavelengths ...” read as a description of “structure,” but “this comet-like tail consists of material ...” is a second independent clause, so the two clauses are joined by a comma alone.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the descriptive phrase runs into the first clause, and “this comet-like tail consists of material ...” then follows with only a comma.

D.why_wrong: “That is visible ...” attaches the phrase to “structure,” but the independent clause “this comet-like tail consists of material ...” still follows with only a comma, so the result is a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: science (astronomy: the ultraviolet tail of the red giant Mira, found in 2007 images from NASA’s GALEX telescope; telescope left unnamed). Band 7: a 10-word adjective-phrase opener that reads as a modifier of “structure” in B, C and D; the splice shows only at “this comet-like tail,” 10 words past the blank; one 47-word run. Menu of 4b424102 (splice, glued, added “that is”); no semicolon option.
band7_moves: 10-word adjective-phrase opener that could modify clause 1’s last noun (“structure”)
clause 2’s subject arrives 10 words past the blank, outside a 6-word window
added-word option (“that is visible”) keeps the splice

fixes: why_wrong B, C and D quoted “this comet-like tail is made of material”; the passage says “consists of material”

band7.why: 4b424102 menu and move: a 10-word adjective-phrase opener reads as a modifier of “structure” in B, C and D, and the splice surfaces only at “this comet-like tail,” 10 words past the blank, in a 47-word run. Every wrong option fails on rule (splice, fused, added words).

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing clause 1 (contrast with the previous sentence), colon before a list
items.passage: Most of the manuscript fragments discovered in the 1890s in the genizah, or storeroom, of a Cairo synagogue come from familiar texts such as prayer books. A few are ______ Hebrew pages of the book of Ben Sira, letters handwritten by Maimonides, and correspondence from merchants who traded with India.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “A few are extraordinary” contrasts with the previous sentence, which says most fragments come from familiar texts, so “however” belongs at the end of this clause, set off by a comma. A colon then introduces the list of extraordinary finds (“Hebrew pages ... correspondence from merchants who traded with India”).

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the list that follows (“Hebrew pages ..., letters ..., and correspondence ...”) isn’t a clause; placing “however” after the semicolon would also wrongly set the list against “A few are extraordinary.”

B.why_wrong: A comma after “however” can’t introduce the list of finds; a colon is needed.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon can’t be used to introduce a list; what follows “however” isn’t an independent clause.

items.notes: Subject: literature and history (Cairo Genizah finds: Hebrew Ben Sira, Maimonides autographs, India-trade letters). Band 7: c15069eb shape. “however” closes clause 1, which answers the previous sentence; A is the taught “; however,” placement. Every distractor fails on a rule because the right side is a three-item list, not a clause (A and C: semicolon before a list; B: comma before a list), so no option fails on meaning alone. No “though” option.
band7_moves: adverb closes clause 1, which contrasts with the previous sentence
taught “; however,” placement offered as the trap, wrong because a list follows
colon variant before a three-item list (c15069eb)

fixes: why_wrong A quoted “and records”; the passage says “and correspondence”
review.attribution: Hebrew Ben Sira, Maimonides autograph letters and India-trade letters among the Cairo Genizah finds read right from recall; kept, not searched

band7.why: c15069eb exactly: “however” closes a clause that answers the previous sentence, then a colon introduces a three-item list. The taught “; however,” placement (A) also fails on rule, since a verbless list follows the semicolon (as in c15069eb’s D); B and C put a comma or semicolon before a list. No option fails on meaning alone.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening clause 2 after a semicolon, with an introductory clause after the adverb
items.passage: In 1957, Nek Chand, a road inspector in Chandigarh, India, began secretly assembling a sculpture garden from broken pottery and other discarded materials. The garden, which officials discovered in 1975, occupied government land without ______ after residents rallied to its defense, the city preserved it and opened it to the public.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The garden ... occupied government land without permission” and “the city preserved it and opened it to the public” are independent clauses. “Even so” signals that the second happened despite the first, so it opens the second clause: a semicolon before it joins the clauses, and a comma after it sets it off from “after residents rallied to its defense.”

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together, and “after residents rallied to its defense” seems to belong to the first one.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join the two independent clauses.

D.why_wrong: With commas on both sides of “even so,” the two independent clauses are still joined by commas alone.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Nek Chand’s Rock Garden, Chandigarh). Band 6: a9e5b788 (3.5) menu, where two options drop the adverb; “even so” opens clause 2 and is followed by a 6-word introductory clause, so the subject “the city” arrives 7 words past the blank. All distractors fail on a rule (fused or splice); no option puts the adverb at the end of clause 1, so nothing fails on meaning alone.

review.attribution: Nek Chand: road inspector, began in 1957 in secret, garden found by officials in 1975 and opened to the public; reads right from recall, kept
review.note: every wrong option fails on a rule (fused, splice, splice); no option puts “even so” at the end of clause 1, so none is wrong by meaning alone

band7.why: Target 6. a9e5b788 (3.5) menu with “even so” opening clause 2, the band-6 adverb shape; the 6-word after-clause puts the subject 7 words past the blank. Every wrong option fails on rule; none is wrong by meaning alone.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a noun phrase whose relative clause holds a finite verb
items.passage: Remoras are fish that attach themselves to sharks, whales, and sea turtles by means of a flattened, oval disc on top of the head. Developmental studies have demonstrated that this disc evolved from an improbable ______ spiny dorsal fin that, in most other fish, stands erect to provide stability during swimming or protection against predators.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Developmental studies have demonstrated that this disc evolved from an improbable source” is a complete clause, and what follows names that source: “the spiny dorsal fin that, in most other fish, stands erect ....” A colon is the mark that introduces such an explanation.

A.why_wrong: “The spiny dorsal fin that, in most other fish, stands erect to provide stability during swimming or protection against predators” is a noun with a relative clause, not a sentence; “stands” belongs to the relative clause, so “fin” has no verb of its own.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “the spiny dorsal fin that, in most other fish, stands erect ...” isn’t one; “stands” belongs to the relative clause.

D.why_wrong: Adding “this was” turns what follows into an independent clause, so the two independent clauses are joined by a comma alone, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: science (the remora’s disc as a modified first dorsal fin, shown by developmental studies; researchers unnamed). Band 7: f30a478e and e9aee0d8 menu (period, semicolon, comma plus added words); the noun phrase after the blank carries a relative clause with a finite verb (“that, in most other fish, stands erect”), with an interrupter as in e9aee0d8, so the period and semicolon versions look like sentences (section 3, move 8). No lone-dash option and no plain comma option (both would be legal).
band7_moves: noun phrase after the colon holds a relative clause with a finite verb (“use”)
period and semicolon options look like complete sentences until the relative clause is parsed
added-word splice (“, this was the”) as in e9aee0d8

fixes: hardened on the e9aee0d8 move: the relative clause in the noun phrase after the colon now opens with an interrupter before its finite verb (“that, in most other fish, stands erect to provide stability during swimming or protection against predators”), so the period and semicolon versions read longer as sentences; cue 19 words past the blank, run from 24 to 31 words; sentence 1 trimmed (“clinging to their hosts” cut) so the passage stays under the models’ median (54 words); explanation, why_wrong A and C, notes updated

band7.why: After the fix, the e9aee0d8 and f30a478e move and menu: the noun phrase after the colon holds a relative clause whose finite verb comes after an interrupter (“that, in most other fish, stands erect ...”), so the period and semicolon versions read as sentences until the passage ends, 19 words past the blank; D adds words to make a splice. Before the fix it sat at the easy edge of 7 (12-word noun phrase).

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a two-item list whose items contain commas
items.passage: To create nierikas, the yarn paintings for which the Wixárika, or Huichol, people of western Mexico are known, an artist needs, besides a wooden board, only two ______ beeswax, which is warmed and spread across the board, and strands of brightly colored yarn, which are carefully pressed into the wax line by line.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “To create nierikas, ... an artist needs, besides a wooden board, only two materials” is a complete clause, and the list that follows (“beeswax, ... and strands of brightly colored yarn, ...”) names the two materials. A colon is used to introduce such a list.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the list after it isn’t a clause; the commas inside the list don’t make a semicolon appropriate here.

B.why_wrong: “Beeswax, which is warmed and spread across the board, and strands of brightly colored yarn, which are carefully pressed into the wax ...” has no main verb, so it can’t stand as a sentence.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the list runs directly into “two materials,” leaving the sentence ungrammatical.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Wixárika yarn paintings). Band 6: c468db1c shape (colon before two named items, each with a which-clause), so the internal commas make a semicolon look right; the which-clauses hold finite verbs (“is warmed,” “are pressed”) that make the period version look like a sentence. Same menu as c468db1c; no dash option.

fixes: why_wrong B quoted “which are pressed into the wax”; the passage says “which are carefully pressed”

band7.why: Target 6. c468db1c shape and menu: two named items after the colon, each with a which-clause, so the internal commas tempt the semicolon and the finite verbs tempt the period. Every wrong option fails on rule.

items.subtype: Restrictive relative clause with that: no punctuation before it
items.passage: Many of the sites settled roughly 3,000 years ago by seafarers who expanded eastward from islands near New Guinea as far as Samoa contain Lapita pottery, a type of ______ use to trace this migration because its stamped geometric designs changed in recognizable ways over time.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “That archaeologists use to trace this migration” is essential to the meaning of “a type of earthenware”: it identifies which earthenware is meant. A restrictive clause like this isn’t set off by punctuation.

B.why_wrong: A comma can’t separate “earthenware” from the restrictive clause “that archaeologists use to trace this migration.”

C.why_wrong: “Archaeologists use to trace this migration ...” lacks an object for “use,” so it isn’t a complete sentence.

D.why_wrong: After the semicolon, “archaeologists use to trace this migration ...” lacks an object for “use,” so it isn’t an independent clause.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Lapita pottery and the settlement of the southwestern Pacific). Band 6: 5ef9fc48 menu (comma before that, period, semicolon). C and D fail because “use” then has no object, which a student sees only at “use to trace,” 2 words past the blank.

band7.why: Target 6. 5ef9fc48 menu (comma before that, period, semicolon); the period and semicolon versions break at “use to trace,” 2 words past the blank, so the cue is local.

items.subtype: Restrictive appositive (title + name) as a subject: no commas around the name or before the verb
items.passage: Before cofounding Mass Observation, a British research project launched in 1937 that recruited volunteers to document the details of everyday life, from shopping habits to conversations overheard in pubs, ______ had lived among communities on Malekula, a South Pacific island in what is now Vanuatu.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Anthropologist” is a title that identifies Tom Harrisson, and the name is essential to it, so no punctuation goes between them. No comma goes after the name either, because “anthropologist Tom Harrisson” is the subject of the verb “had lived.”

A.why_wrong: The commas set off “Tom Harrisson” as if it were extra information, but the name is essential to the title “anthropologist” and to the subject of “had lived.”

B.why_wrong: The comma after “Harrisson” separates the subject from its verb, “had lived.”

D.why_wrong: The comma separates the title “anthropologist” from the name it introduces.

items.notes: Subject: social science (Mass Observation, 1937; Tom Harrisson had lived on Malekula in the New Hebrides in the 1930s before cofounding it with Charles Madge and Humphrey Jennings). Band 7: 5aae2475 menu (all four comma placements around title + name); one 45-word run in which the title follows a long introductory phrase that holds an appositive and ends in a comma, so a comma pair looks natural, and the verb right after the name tempts a closing comma.
band7_moves: title + name followed directly by the verb, which tempts a closing comma
the slot follows an introductory phrase’s comma, so a comma pair looks natural

review.attribution: Tom Harrisson lived on Malekula (New Hebrides) in the 1930s before cofounding Mass Observation in 1937; reads right from recall, kept

band7.why: 5aae2475 menu (all four comma placements around title plus name) after a 30-word introductory phrase full of commas that ends in a comma, so a comma pair around the name looks natural and the verb right after the name tempts a closing comma; 45-word run.

items.subtype: Opening dash of a pair whose element holds a series and an absolute phrase
items.passage: Because building stone is scarce along the low-lying coasts of Georgia and South Carolina, builders there relied from the 1700s onward on ______ concrete made of sand, water, lime, and whole oyster shells, the lime itself produced by burning still more shells—to construct houses, fortifications, and warehouses.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The element “a concrete made of sand, water, lime, and whole oyster shells, the lime itself produced by burning still more shells” describes tabby and is closed by the dash after “shells.” A matching dash is needed after “tabby” to open it, so that “relied ... on tabby” connects with “to construct houses, fortifications, and warehouses.”

A.why_wrong: The element is closed by a dash after “shells,” so it can’t be opened with a comma; the commas inside the element don’t change that.

C.why_wrong: A colon can’t open an element that a dash then closes in the middle of the sentence.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “tabby a concrete” runs together, and the dash after “shells” has no partner.

items.notes: Subject: history (tabby, the oyster-shell concrete of the colonial Georgia and South Carolina coast). Band 7: 109d5bbb shape, the blank opens the pair and the partner dash comes 19 words later; the element holds a four-item series and an absolute phrase, so its many commas make the comma option look like a comma pair (6e071432’s two levels). No partner is visible near the blank.
band7_moves: blank opens the pair; partner dash 19 words later
second level inside the element: a series and an absolute phrase full of commas
comma option looks like a comma pair until the closing dash

band7.why: 109d5bbb menu (colon, dash, comma, none) with the 6e071432 second level: the dash element holds a four-item series and an absolute phrase, so the comma option looks like a comma pair, and the partner dash comes 19 words after the blank.

items.subtype: Semicolons between series items that contain commas, plus the comma before an item’s appositive
items.passage: In mid-twentieth-century Japan, storytellers performed kamishibai, or “paper theater,” for children on city streets. A storyteller’s equipment typically included a bicycle, which transported everything from place to ______ small wooden stage that framed the illustrations; and a stack of hand-painted cards, which he slid out while narrating.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The items in this series contain commas (“a bicycle, which transported ...,” “a butai, a small wooden stage ...”), so semicolons separate the items, as the semicolon before “and a stack” shows. A semicolon therefore goes after “place,” and a comma goes between “a butai” and the appositive that explains it, “a small wooden stage that framed the illustrations.”

A.why_wrong: A comma after “place” doesn’t match the semicolon that separates the next items, and it blurs where the first item ends.

B.why_wrong: The semicolon is right, but without a comma after “butai,” the appositive “a small wooden stage that framed the illustrations” runs into the noun it explains.

C.why_wrong: A colon can’t separate one series item from the next.

items.notes: Subject: arts (kamishibai street storytelling; butai is the wooden frame). Band 7: 9c3630b9 shape, blank spans the end of item 1 and the start of item 2 with two slots of different rules (series semicolon, appositive comma); the revealing semicolon comes 7 words after the blank; B is right at the first slot and wrong at the second, A the reverse.
band7_moves: two slots of different rules in one option (series semicolon, appositive comma)
revealing semicolon comes 7 words past the blank
each partly right option matches the key at one slot

fixes: sentence 1 reworded (“storytellers performed kamishibai, or “paper theater,” for children”) so the gloss no longer splits the compound “kamishibai storytellers”; tested boundary untouched

band7.why: 9c3630b9 shape: the blank spans the end of item 1 and the start of item 2 with two slots under different rules (series semicolon, appositive comma); the revealing semicolon comes 7 words after the blank, and A and B are each right at one slot.

items.subtype: Comma pair around a conjunctive adverb between an introductory clause and the main clause
items.passage: Most freshwater fish perish quickly if the ponds or streams they inhabit dry up. As its pool shrinks during the dry ______ an African lungfish burrows into the mud and encases itself in a cocoon of hardened mucus, breathing air through a small opening until the rains return.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “As its pool shrinks during the dry season” is an introductory clause, and “an African lungfish burrows into the mud ...” is the main clause. “However” is a supplementary element between them, so it is set off by a pair of commas.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “As its pool shrinks during the dry season” is a dependent clause.

C.why_wrong: “As its pool shrinks during the dry season.” is a dependent clause, so it can’t stand as a sentence.

D.why_wrong: The semicolon separates the introductory clause “As its pool shrinks during the dry season, however” from the main clause it introduces.

items.notes: Subject: science (African lungfish estivating in mucus cocoons). Plan cell asked for band 7, but S3_comma_pair has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/boundaries.md appendix), so it is written as a strong band 6 and band_target is 6. Shape: the S3_adverb_pair intro-clause variant (e3c1b4f7); B and D are the taught “; however,” / “, however;” clause-joining placements, and all three distractors fail on a rule because no independent clause precedes the blank. “However” contrasts with sentence 1.

review.note: every wrong option fails on a rule: “As its pool shrinks during the dry season” is dependent, so no semicolon or period can follow it; none is wrong by meaning alone

band7.why: The plan asked for band 7, but S3_comma_pair has no band-7 official items, so it is held at a strong band 6. Its shape is the e3c1b4f7 adverb-pair move (intro clause, “however,” main clause, with the taught “; however,” and “, however;” offered), so it may read harder than 6. Every wrong option fails on rule.

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: Because carrying strings of copper coins home was risky, many Tang dynasty merchants who sold goods in China’s capital began in the early 800s to deposit their coins with provincial offices there in exchange for paper ______ these could be redeemed for coins in the merchants’ home provinces.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Many Tang dynasty merchants ... began in the early 800s to deposit their coins ... in exchange for paper certificates” and “these could be redeemed for coins in the merchants’ home provinces” are independent clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: No comma is needed after “and” here; the comma before it is enough to join the two independent clauses.

B.why_wrong: When “and” joins two independent clauses like these, a comma is needed before it.

D.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join two independent clauses.

items.notes: Subject: history (Tang dynasty flying money, early ninth century). 1.31 and 2.2 menus (comma after the conjunction, conjunction without comma, splice); one 48-word sentence with an introductory because-clause, and both joined clauses are long, so the comma-less “and” is not acceptable.

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a short participial phrase
items.passage: The sandbox tree, which grows in tropical forests of the Americas, disperses its seeds explosively. As each pumpkin-shaped fruit dries, tension accumulates in its woody walls until the fruit ruptures with a sound resembling a ______ this way, the seeds can land remarkably far from the parent tree.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “As each pumpkin-shaped fruit dries, tension accumulates ... with a sound resembling a gunshot” is a complete sentence. “Launched this way” describes “the seeds,” the subject of the next sentence (“the seeds can land remarkably far from the parent tree”), so a period is needed after “gunshot.”

A.why_wrong: The comma attaches “launched this way” to the first clause, leaving “the seeds can land remarkably far from the parent tree” joined to it by a comma alone.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “gunshot launched this way” runs the two sentences together, and the second independent clause follows only a comma.

C.why_wrong: “And” can’t join the phrase “launched this way” to the first clause, and “the seeds can land ...” still follows only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: science (the sandbox tree, Hura crepitans, and its exploding fruit). Medium: a 3-word participial opener (“Launched this way”), as in 2.9 and 2.27 (2 to 3 word openers).

items.subtype: Closing comma of a pair around a participial appositive phrase
items.passage: Women in the Mithila region of India and Nepal have traditionally decorated the walls of their homes with elaborate paintings of deities, animals, and plants. In 1934, William Archer, a British official surveying damage from an ______ discovered such paintings on the exposed interior walls of collapsed houses.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “A British official surveying damage from an earthquake” is a supplementary element that describes William Archer, and it is opened by the comma after “Archer.” A matching comma after “earthquake” closes it, so that the subject “William Archer” connects to its verb, “discovered.”

B.why_wrong: Without a closing comma, the element opened after “Archer” is never closed, and “earthquake discovered such paintings” reads as if the earthquake did the discovering.

C.why_wrong: The element is opened with a comma, so it can’t be closed with a dash.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon can’t separate the subject “William Archer” from its verb, “discovered.”

items.notes: Subject: arts (Mithila, or Madhubani, painting brought to wider notice after the 1934 Bihar earthquake). The partner comma sits 7 words before the blank (2.1 and 2.6 shape).

review.attribution: William Archer, British official in Bihar, saw Mithila wall paintings after the 1934 earthquake; reads right from recall, kept

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: Strangler figs often germinate high in the rainforest canopy from seeds that birds or bats deposit on the branches of other trees. As a young fig grows, it sends roots to the soil and gradually encircles the host’s ______ the tree of sunlight and nutrients, often until the host dies.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “As a young fig grows, it sends roots to the soil and gradually encircles the host’s trunk” is a complete clause, and “depriving the tree of sunlight and nutrients” is a participial phrase that describes the effect of that action. A comma separates such a trailing phrase from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “depriving the tree of sunlight and nutrients” is a phrase without a subject and main verb.

C.why_wrong: “Depriving the tree of sunlight and nutrients, often until the host dies.” isn’t a complete sentence.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, “trunk depriving the tree” makes it seem that the trunk is doing the depriving.

items.notes: Subject: science (strangler figs). 2.4 and 2.26 shape: a trailing -ing phrase after a complete clause; menu semicolon, period, no mark.

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory adjective phrase
items.passage: Home to one of the largest markets in West ______ the Nigerian city of Onitsha became the center of a thriving trade in inexpensive pamphlets after World War II, as local authors wrote about everything from romance to politics.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Home to one of the largest markets in West Africa” is an introductory phrase that describes the subject of the sentence, “the Nigerian city of Onitsha.” A comma is needed to separate this introductory phrase from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: Without a comma, the introductory phrase runs into the subject, “the Nigerian city of Onitsha.”

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “Home to one of the largest markets in West Africa” is a phrase.

D.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, but “Home to one of the largest markets in West Africa” isn’t one.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Onitsha market literature, Nigeria, after 1945). 2.25 shape: an introductory phrase describing the subject, then the subject.

items.subtype: Semicolon between independent clauses
items.passage: In the nineteenth century, Chinook Jargon, a trade language that drew on Chinook, Nuu-chah-nulth, French, and English, was widely spoken along the Pacific coast from Oregon to Alaska. Its vocabulary was limited, perhaps only a few hundred ______ speakers stretched those words to express an impressive variety of meanings.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Its vocabulary was limited, perhaps only a few hundred words” and “speakers stretched those words to express an impressive variety of meanings” are independent clauses. A semicolon is used to join two independent clauses that are closely related.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join two independent clauses.

C.why_wrong: When “and” joins two independent clauses like these, a comma is needed before it.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

items.notes: Subject: language (Chinook Jargon, the trade language of the Pacific Northwest). 2.22 menu without its added “later”; no period option (official rule) and no “, and” option (legal twin). Origin and use only, no revival frame.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: Scattered along a beach on New Zealand’s South Island, the Moeraki Boulders are nearly perfect spheres, some approximately two meters across. They began forming roughly 60 million years ago ______ sediment on the seafloor, as minerals gradually cemented the mud into hardened concretions.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Sediment on the seafloor” is the object of the preposition “within.” No punctuation should separate a preposition from its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon can’t separate the preposition “within” from its object.

B.why_wrong: A comma can’t separate the preposition “within” from its object.

C.why_wrong: A dash can’t separate the preposition “within” from its object.

items.notes: Subject: science (geology: the Moeraki Boulders, concretions formed in seafloor mud).

items.subtype: No punctuation between a verb and its object
items.passage: Dated to 1728, Utendi wa Tambuka is one of the earliest known works of Swahili poetry. Written in Arabic script, the epic ______ a seventh-century conflict between Muslim forces and the Byzantine Empire in more than a thousand stanzas.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “A seventh-century conflict between Muslim forces and the Byzantine Empire” is the object of the verb “describes.” No punctuation should separate a verb from its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon can’t separate the verb “describes” from its object.

C.why_wrong: A comma can’t separate the verb “describes” from its object.

D.why_wrong: A dash can’t separate the verb “describes” from its object.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Utendi wa Tambuka, an early Swahili epic).

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: Nearly all shipworms, clams with long, wormlike bodies, tunnel into ______ a species discovered in 2019 in a river in the Philippines bores into solid limestone, swallowing fragments of rock as it digs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Nearly all shipworms ... tunnel into wood” and “a species discovered in 2019 ... bores into solid limestone” are independent clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: When “but” joins two independent clauses like these, a comma is needed before it.

B.why_wrong: No comma is needed after “but”; the comma before it is enough to join the two independent clauses.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation or conjunction, the two independent clauses run together.

items.notes: Subject: science (the rock-boring shipworm Lithoredo abatanica, described in 2019). 1.31 menu; a one-sentence item, and the second clause is long, so the comma-less “but” is not acceptable.

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory subordinate clause (it also closes an appositive)
items.passage: After disease, emigration, and increasing isolation had steadily reduced the population of St Kilda, a remote group of islands far off Scotland’s west ______ the last 36 residents asked the British government to evacuate them, and in August 1930 they left.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “After disease, emigration, and increasing isolation had steadily reduced the population of St Kilda, a remote group of islands far off Scotland’s west coast” is an introductory subordinate clause, and “the last 36 residents asked the British government to evacuate them” begins the main clause. A comma is needed between them; it also closes the description of St Kilda opened by the comma after “Kilda.”

B.why_wrong: Without a comma, the introductory clause runs into the main clause, and the description of St Kilda is never closed.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the introductory “After ...” clause is a dependent clause.

D.why_wrong: “After disease, emigration, and increasing isolation had steadily reduced the population of St Kilda, ... west coast.” is a dependent clause, so it can’t stand as a sentence.

items.notes: Subject: history (the 1930 evacuation of St Kilda). 1.6 and 1.19 shape: a long introductory After clause, one 41-word sentence.

items.subtype: Direct question after a question word: inverted order and question mark
items.passage: In the early 1800s, Boston merchant Frederic Tudor began shipping ice harvested from New England ponds to customers as far away as India. How ______ Tudor packed the blocks tightly in sawdust, an inexpensive insulating material that dramatically slowed melting.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the ice survived such long journeys?
did the ice survive such long journeys.
the ice survived such long journeys.
did the ice survive such long journeys?
items.explanation: The sentence beginning with “How” is a direct question, so it needs question word order (“did the ice survive”) and a question mark. The next sentence answers it.

A.why_wrong: A direct question needs question word order (“did the ice survive”), not statement order.

B.why_wrong: The word order is right for a direct question, but a direct question must end with a question mark.

C.why_wrong: This is a direct question, so it needs question word order and a question mark, not statement order and a period.

items.notes: Subject: history (Frederic Tudor’s ice trade). 1.18 and 1.30 shape: a direct question opened by How, answered in the next sentence.

items.subtype: Commas between items of a simple series
items.passage: Tuatara, reptiles found only in New Zealand, are the last surviving members of a group that flourished during the age of the dinosaurs. They remain active at temperatures too cold for most ______ grow extremely slowly, and can live for more than a century.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three things tuatara do: “remain active at temperatures too cold for most reptiles,” “grow extremely slowly,” and “can live for more than a century.” Commas separate the items in a simple series like this one, so a comma is needed after “reptiles,” the end of the first item.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon isn’t used to separate items in a simple series whose items contain no commas.

C.why_wrong: Without a comma, the first item runs into the second (“too cold for most reptiles grow extremely slowly”), and the sentence no longer makes sense; a comma must separate the items, as one does before “and.”

D.why_wrong: A colon can’t be used to separate items in a series.

items.notes: Subject: science (tuatara). 1.12 shape: a series of verb phrases, blank after the first item (moved in review from the serial-comma slot).

fixes: second defensible option: with the blank at the serial-comma slot, C (“slowly and can live”) gave a series without the optional serial comma, acceptable in standard written English and invisible to rw_options; blank moved to after item 1 (“too cold for most ______ grow extremely slowly, and”), as in 1.3, 1.12 and 1.25; options now reptiles; / reptiles, / reptiles / reptiles:, key still B; explanation, why_wrong and notes rewritten
review.note: blind solve matched the key (B) but flagged C as defensible; fixed by construction

items.subtype: Restrictive relative clause with that: no punctuation before it
items.passage: Japan is home to an unusually large number of companies that have operated for centuries. The oldest may have been Kongō Gumi, a ______ built and repaired Buddhist temples from 578 CE until 2006, when financial difficulties led to its absorption by a larger construction company.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “That built and repaired Buddhist temples from 578 CE until 2006 ...” is essential to the meaning of “a firm”: it tells what kind of firm Kongō Gumi was. A restrictive clause like this isn’t set off by punctuation, and “that” is needed as the subject of “built and repaired.”

A.why_wrong: Without “that,” nothing serves as the subject of “built and repaired,” so the sentence is ungrammatical.

B.why_wrong: A comma can’t separate “firm” from the restrictive clause that describes it.

D.why_wrong: Without “that,” “a firm built and repaired Buddhist temples” has no subject for “built and repaired.”

items.notes: Subject: social science (business history: Kongō Gumi, the temple builder founded in 578). 1.29 menu (comma, comma + that, that, nothing), with a different frame (“a firm that built and repaired”).
